editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Ernest C. Sweigert. Mr. Sweigert served in the U.S. Army and Army Air Corps. He served in the European Theater. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Sweigert's home in Mentor, Ohio, on July 6th, 2004. Ernest was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: 1941, I was living in good ole Clermont, which is part of the old Nottingham section of Cleveland, when I was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you still in high school in '41?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I graduated in '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In June of '41 or --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: June 16th, 19 -- June 17th, 1941. And I was looking forward to a whole summer of relaxation on the beach at Wildwood Park. And my dad had other ideas, being an old German. And he says, "Oh, no." So June 30th I started with Towmotor Corporation on 152nd Street, and worked there until summoned for the good old Army in 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it wasn't a summer job; you took a regular job?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I took a regular job. I started off in the blueprint department of the -- engineering. And after about six months or so, seven months, they gave me a little board to do redraws of old drawings that needed to be updated, and in the process made blueprints for the shop and so forth. And eventually went on to the board in the last six months before going into Service in February. So that was my background.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Not really. The only thing I can recall, I was driving around on that particular day and heard it on the car radio. But nothing significant as far as the December 7th at all. To me, anyway. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And there was no feeling of, gee, maybe I better go sign up now?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No, no. You have to realize, my mother was antiwar. She didn't like the Navy because she was afraid of water. She thought the Marine Corps was a _____; you'd get yourself killed. And she didn't want me to fly, and I wanted to fly. And so I had to take no choice but let the Army put me where they want -- what they wanted to give me. So that's where I went. So as I say, Mother was not -- at that time, only being 19 or 20 -- in '40 -- I'll be 20 in '43. You had to have your signature -- mother's -- parents' -- or father --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: -- sign for you to go into the Air Corps. You could go into the Army but not the Air Corps. So that was a drawback.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything for the war effort in that year or so before you went in?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Well, I was working, as I said, for Towmotor Lift Trucks, and we had the -- got the E award, you know, for excellence and all that. So in essence, I was working in a war plant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That wasn't --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But not enough to give you a deferment?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh, no. A young kid like that? No. See, my dad had worked at Towmotor back in -- started back in '32, '33. So it was a continuation into the process of me coming in. And I took care of my summer lying on the beach. And so June 30th, 1941 started the longest summer job I had ever had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Was rationing much of a problem in that time, in '41?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No. Because up to '4 -- up to going in, rationing wasn't really in effect. I found one little booklet here but -- that my mother had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I also delivered the mail, picked up the mail at a common post office. So I had a B ticket on my car, so I had a little more gas than the average guy. Tires were my problem.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But no, it -- Pearl Harbor came. My mother and -- you know, she would talk, "No way, no way, no way, no way." But her father was Swedish and they -- he left Sweden with the intent he did not believe in military training, automatic, like they have in Switzerland. So he figured he was going to raise his family in the good old USA. And that's -- so my mother inherited that antiwar thinking all the way around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And Pearl Harbor didn't change her mind about that?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No. Pearl Harbor -- matter of fact, you know, it's funny. Because when we -- on the German side of the family, my dad, I swear he was still born in Germany, but they say -- claim he never was. But all his sisters were, that were older, and they came over. But he enlisted in World War I at -- how old was he? 1888 -- 29 years of age, and he was in the Air Corps, a mechanic, and he got to France. So even -- at that point he was -- if he had been up in the front, he could have been fighting against his own cousins and brothers and so forth. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I was sworn in on the 12th of February, went in the Service, Camp Perry, on the 22nd. The coldest damn month I ever spent up at Camp Perry. I can't -- never forget it. We got up there and we got our, you know, clothing and everything. And I ended up on the wood detail. I can't remember what my job was, holding up _____+. And we carried all the old wood up to the Sandusky Old Soldiers' Home. And we went over there and would make our trip back. And that wind blew. The temperature was down in the teens and below zero at night. And the first week, when we came back, we were all promised weekend passes. And rode the truck around -- instead of getting off and hopping off the CQ quarters, I rode around in front -- fifth in the front, when they said, "That's all the passes we have for you." So I got real smart and I said, okay, I'll be a furnace guard and -- to keep the fires going in the barracks, and that way I can get over first thing, you know, and make it with no problem at all, thinking -- so that week I signed up for that furnace detail. The only thing wrong, they cut papers. So it never materialized. We were given orders to go and that was it. So I didn't get home until a lot later. So from there, from Camp Perry, which was basically February, I ended up in Fort Useless, Virginia -- you know, I said "Useless." It is Eustis, E-u-s-t i-s -- in March, and ended up with -- being given some more equipment, including a 1918 helmet -- we didn't have the new bucket helmets yet -- and ended up assigned to the 90th millimeter anti-aircraft battery. And my first sergeant, I -- he was the only one I remember the name, was Sergeant Bale, an old regular Army guy, and got to know him quite well because I could never march worth a damn. And he'd always have me up as a point guard and break ranks and have me come back and walk with him at the back of the platoon. So -- but one of our things there, back in -- went out to the rifle range and came back with a collapsed lung, which was miserable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: The pain was excruciating. But I went on the obstacle course, ran the obstacle course. But if I can say run, it was not the case. I dragged myself all the way through it. And the following morning I signed up for sick leave -- sick call, and thought, you know, I'll make it. And I get down there, sat there, and the guy came over and he says, "What did you guys do, have an obstacle course?" I said, "Yeah, we had an obstacle course." He said, "Oh, I see all of you guys come in here off the obstacle course." Well, he went on down the line and he listened to me and he -- "Oh, oh, oh. You wait here." So I waited. And finally the lieutenant came in just about -- oh, probably about 11:30, just before chow time and he listened to me. "Uh-huh, uh-huh, uh-huh. Okay." And he wrote out a slip. Report to the hospital on base. So I got back to the -- for lunch and then went on and saw the first sergeant and said, "I'm supposed to report to the hospital after lunch." Well, at "Fort Useless" our barracks were here. I had to go across the parade grounds to get to the hospital all the time. Got in there and they did X-rays, and came back out and sat down with Major Goldfire (ph) and he says, "You've got pneumothorax," which in plain language was a collapsed lung. And he shown me my X-ray, and it looked like a cat had gown down, claw marks, all streaks. And he said, "What do you -- how do you think -- what caused it?" I says, "Well, maybe I had my sling too tight out on the firing range and something happened." I mean, that was the only thing I could think of. Well, needless to say, with that, I ended up in a ward without ever getting back, no -- just the clothes on my back, no toothbrush, no nothing. So they sent the stuff over, giving instructions. You don't get out of bed with pneumothorax. Complete rest. No tube like they have down -- nowadays to keep your lung compressed. And so anyhow, I spent 18 days in the hospital, and I kept chomping at the bit to get back to the outfit. And when they released me after 18 days, got back, Sergeant Bale (ph) looked at me and he said, "You" -- called me sort of a dumbass. He said, "Three more days, you'd have had a convalescent furlough back home." And he says, "You missed the equivalent of three weeks." He says, "We can't keep you. You're no longer going to be with us." So I was then transferred over to a 40mm Bofor gun outfit. It was comprised of 1B classifications, civilians, not quite very many, but they were trying to see how many they could keep. So I spent a couple of weeks there. In the meantime I had written home while I was still in the 90th before, that the way the sergeant had talked, we were going to ship down the James River, right overseas, as soon as we completed our basic. So I talked my mother into going around and getting my five recommendations from people for the Air Corps. So I see -- I saw the president and owner of Towmotor, Mr. Sears, and he signed. And a neighbor next door, Mr. Asadorian (ph), he was an inspector for the government, and he signed. And a fellow down the street, worked for Oliver Corporation, he signed. And then I had my high school teacher sign up. So I had all my -- so in the process, I got transferred out of the Bofors outfit, and we went up to what we called the CC camp while we were waiting for shipment papers to come in. And what we did up there was clean -- clean officers' barracks, or KP for two weeks. So it turned out that I ended up going down to Keesler Field, Mississippi, in May of '43 and got, you know -- so I ended up down there waiting for -- going through the classification system and so forth. And what they were doing, you got more tests, needless to say, and they -- finally they determined I was going to go to the -- what college -- it was University of Tennessee. So I ended up at the University of Tennessee from June '43 through September '43, and all we did was study. I thought I had a great place. We were in the gym. We were bivouacked in the gym, overlooking the football field. I said, "Oh, knowing the University of Tennessee, oh great." I'm -- because -- I never got into football because that's the year Tennessee dropped football. So we finished up there and got sent down to Nashville for testing to know whether you're going to be a pilot navigator or bombardier, and spent a couple of weeks in Nashville and then ended up in Decatur -- Decatur -- Maxwell Field October through February '44. But luckily, in January of '44 I did get a furlough from down there to come home, and I got home for ten days before going back down. And in the interim, everything was backed up in the Air Corps system. So my class of 44G became 44H, which meant we were extended one month down the pipe. One of the odd things that happened in the Maxwell Field deal, all of a sudden they decided all cadets have to learn how to drill. Well, being out of the ground forces, I was called an aviation student, not a cadet, but I had also done the manual arms. So we went -- all marched over to the warehouse and picked up Enfield rifles, which are British-made rifles, loaded with Cosmoline from World War I, in storage there. When I -- so we had a -- having been in the ground forces otherwise, I fieldstripped my gun in the shower with hot water. And a few of us had -- like myself, knew what we were doing. So then we ended up being drill instructors for the rest of the cadets who had not had it. So anyhow, finished up at Maxwell and got papers signed. We were shipped up to Decatur, Alabama which is on the northern tip of Alabama, where Montgomery is down in the south portion, and we took up flying up there. And we were assigned into groups of four cadets to a pilot. And I had -- I flew with a fellow named Harvey Watts and -- quite a fellow, six-foot two, 200 and some-odd pounds, jovial-looking son of a gun, but he was -- he could be otherwise too. And so I went through that and flew PT-17s, and had some experiences which I look back on with fond memory at the time. But I ground-looped a plane on a crosswind landing, which was one thing. I can remember my first solo. He took -- Harvey came out, took me -- he'd taxi up to the end of the takeoff area. And he says, "Hold it here," he says. "I'm getting out." He says, "I don't want to be embarrassed by your maneuvers getting off the ground." And he sat out there and he said, "Make two passes around the field and come back down and pick me up if you survive." And that was Harvey. I can remember I screwed up on -- doing something one day, and he said to me, "You know, what did you do, join the Air Corps just to get the hell out of Service so you wouldn't have to go overseas?" He was that type of guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I -- we did shots on one occasion, in both arms, double booster shots, and I was -- and I was having a hell of a hard time. I was aching. And he said, "What kind of a pilot do you want to be?" I says, "Well, I want to be an attack bomber." He says, "Well, I'll show you how to buzz the fence down there." "What, are you chicken? I said buzz the fence." Now, we went down to the level, grass-top level, hedgehopped over the farmers' fences down there. Took it up. He spotted a duck. And I can't -- he denies it. But I talked to him years later. He chased this mallard, and, I mean, he was all over there. And I'm, "Whoo." And he come up -- he came up after this duck and it was going between a stand of pine trees. He had to do a wing-up in order to get through without leaving the wings behind. And he denies he ever did that. But I remember very distinctly, "I think I'm going to leave two wings behind." So anyhow, we got through that. I lost one of the fellows in the -- our group. The best pilot -- potential pilot was a fellow named Bud Atkinson from Hawaii. He soloed in seven and a half hours. My buddy, Chuck Schroeder, soloed around 8:50, eight hours and 50 minutes, and I went out at 9:15. We finished up our 65 hours in primary. And one of the things which we did, on the last day I took her up to 4500 feet. I set the record for spins, 14 spins. Chuck thought she was -- hell, I had bought it. I came out at about 200 feet and I saw Chuck was heading back. So, boy, I -- I figured he's reporting. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say you lost one of the guys during that training?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. He -- well, I say lost. He was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Washed out?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Washed out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, he got washed out. A big -- big Irish man. He was -- our group was set up by size, with the exception of Atkinson. I didn't think he was -- Schroeder and I and -- because he was -- all of us were six-footers. That's -- one of the things we had to do was have a picture taken when we got done at the University of Tennessee. The colonel had a -- I'm certain he got a percentage on the -- for promoting. Now, that's Chuck. Chuck was married. And so he had his wife travel around with him, which was unusual. And that's the old boy Harvey Watts. You notice the term he had for me? Strong heart. But -- and so we finished up and got out of there, and when we got back to the field after spinning, I almost landed right on his tail. I said, "Chuck, I didn't want you going over and telling the old man that I had spun in." And he says, "Well, you sure as hell scared the hell out of me like you did the other day when you snap-rolled around me." But we used to do some stupid things. When you were soloing, you were in the backseat. And the shoulder straps should have been buckled in front. I can remember diving on the barges on the Gunner Field Dam and the straps came over and hit me in the head, And again, with my buddy flying along the side me, so it made me go down inside. He wondered what the heck happened. Well, I was down there grabbing the -- hooking them in so they wouldn't do anything. We did that. We chased -- I can remember chasing a farmer, trying to get his donkey, or jackass, into the barn. And I pointed -- and he says, "Yeah." I buzzed the old thing, and it went right to the barn. So that's the good parts of -- so we went from there, graduated -- by the way, that was -- that -- when Decatur was -- the school was called Southeast Flying Training Command. And they gave you a nice diploma when you finished up your training there. And we went 40 miles down the road to a place called Courtland, Alabama, and that was the basic flying school there. And I got 15 hours in then, and that's when I got my wings clipped in the end of May. At that point, the Army was -- military was needing back guys from -- and it seemed like all aviation students were getting their wings clipped to go back into the ranks. So at the end of May, after about 15 hours, I had my papers. The -- I was washed out with about 200 guys out of our class. They only kept about 35 or 40 of them. And the next thing I knew, I was down in Camp Shelby, Alabama, Hattiesburg -- I said Alabama. Camp Shelby, Mississippi. Hattiesburg, a town of about 10,000, with a hundred thousand troops in the field next door. And now if you ask me when D-Day was, I can tell you exactly. I was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were there?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I heard the arguments between the artillery boys and the infantry boys. And the artillery guys were getting hell from the infantry guys about, "I wouldn't have been here if it hadn't been for you guys having a short fuse. I got the shrapnel in my back from you guys' friendly fire back in '43." So I spent a couple of weeks there, got assigned to Camp Rucker, Alabama, combat -- 288th Combat Engineers. And got in there just before the weekend, and I had went up on the weekend to play softball -- football. And I put my khaki shirts on from the Air Corps and went out and joined up with a bunch of other guys wearing their tan shirts, and we played football against the -- and the next morning, fall out in ranks, and you should have seen these officers' mouths all drop. "You're a private and you were playing with us?" They just looked at the shirts and figured I was another officer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So anyhow, Lieutenant Stuck was my platoon commander down there. But Captain Stone called me in the office and he said, "You know, I'm a West Pointer." He said, "I got washed out with just about the same amount of hours in basic as you have." And he said, "You know," he said, "We're making up cadres, a company -- we're draft -- we're taking people from every branch of service that we don't need anymore." And one of the branches of service was A and E aircraft of all things, which I had started out in. We had noncoms. We had -- if we had one corporal, we had 20 corporals. We had 15 buck sergeants, staff sergeants, and two first sergeants. I mean, we were rolling with noncomps. And they -- he said, "I'm going to send you to the first school that becomes available." He says -- I said, "Okay," you know. Well, it turned out to be cook and baker school. And I'll be damned if I didn't remember what I did there. But I was sent to Fort Benning, Georgia, paratrooper school, and I ended up in the paratrooper barracks. And I used to go to school and then come back up here. And when the guys were running and I didn't -- I wasn't -- and didn't have class, I'd run with them, which -- part of the old training. They'd used to think I was nuts running. "What in the hell are you doing that for?" I said, "Well, did it in the Service, you know, at Rucker, and I want to keep my body up." So we did that. Come back, and we had more cooks than we needed in Alabama, so we had three-day shifts, one -- work one day out of every three. But there was no place to go. There was no towns around Camp Rucker at that time. There was -- I can name them, but they were all eight, ten thousand at the most, and they were -- you know, see, you didn't do anything. You just basically wolfed around. We had a swimming pool in the area so we did that. And finally we got -- papers were cut that we were going to go overseas in October, so in September I got -- they gave me a four-day leave. Four days was the minimum you could have. And I'm down in Alabama and I've got to get to Cleveland. Well, the other thing was a mistake. You need -- I needed to go through an infiltration course. So you had to go through the infiltration course. Well, I didn't -- my first day was -- I didn't get out of Camp Rucker until nine o'clock that evening. So in essence, I had spent 21 hours of my first day of my furlough in -- got -- I had 36 hours in Cleveland. And I just said, "I wished to hell I had more guts. I'd have taken a couple." But you live by the law, and I had 36 hours up here to bid adieu to everybody, if you can say that, and of course girlfriend, and it was a little more time with her than I think that I -- than I had with my own parents. So we went back down and we shipped up to Camp Shanks, New York, for a staging area up there. That was October. And we shipped out of Camp Shanks. What did you do in Camp Shanks? Of course I was cooking. And we shipped out of Camp Shanks on October 22nd and went down to New York City, got on the USS Argentina, which happened to be the commodore ship in going over. Our shipping orders were 9945C. I remember those. And we were supposed to end up in Cherbourg, but the Jerrys sank so many ships in the harbor, this ship couldn't get in. So we got to be sent over to a place called Swansea, Wales, arriving on the 6th of November.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And did you go alone, or were you in a convoy?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh, we went in a convoy. Oh, yeah. Nothing went alone except the Queen Mary.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Only the fast ones.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, Queen Mary.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And we had only one alert going over. Anyhow, it was -- we carried about 15,000, I guess, on that. And I had top bunk of four layers, ate two meals a day. One of the things we had done -- Norm Swanstrom was my buddy. He's another Swede, background from Minnesota. And I had bought about three or four packets of Fig Newtons in the PX before, you know. And there -- from morning breakfast till late, we'd open a box -- eat two or three Fig Newtons in the middle of the day, sitting up on deck. We had one alert, broad daylight, and everything was interesting because everything -- the ship all of a sudden was leaning at about a 30-degree angle because it was out -- breaking course. And the upsiders went off and they were -- got -- DEs were chasing whatever they were chasing out there. But we got over to England, in Swansea, and we trained down to a place called Bristol down in the moors, in Dartmoor, and -- you can remember Sherlock Holmes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And we were in Romney huts, which are old metal curved huts, and we were on the colonel's property, which of course -- and when I got in there, one -- the first time we went out of town, the guy said, "You know, the last group that was in there was colored troops." He said, "You guys are fun but what -- before that, we had the 29th Division. That was their staging area down there." So I was no longer cooking, per se. I was now -- from headquarters I was in a platoon learning what engineers are supposed to do, except at Christmastime and Thanksgiving time I was pulled back in to be another helpful cook. You know, you get your frozen turkeys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And you had to thaw them out and so on and so forth. So anyhow, I did that and then we went into a working group. And we stayed there in Southern England and we went over to Torquay. It was -- we were running pontoon bridges across. We spent a couple of nights down there. And of course, January '44 was a miserable time, snow in England as well as the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '45 right?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Starting in December. Right?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. So we ended up -- we had guys coming in, saying we -- we were out taking -- practiced rolling in the snow, you know, an infantry tact. And the guy said, "Wouldn't you like to volunteer?" I said, "No." Stay with the old unit, though. Never, never volunteer. Stay with the unit. So we went up from there. We got out of Bristol, and they shipped us over to a place called Weston-super-Mare, about 20 miles or so from Bristol, England. And there we did more training. And matter of fact, that was my second stint in the hospital. When I -- I went out firing a bazooka and got propellant charges in my eye. Boy, that was another miserable -- that was about as painful, if not more, than the collapsed lung. I had a handkerchief. I came back, any air striking that eye was pitiful. Got back about five o'clock in camp. Went over to see a Greek doctor. He said, "Don't bother me. I'm going to supper now. You come back and see me after supper." And I said, "I got" -- you know, I don't -- an arrogant SOB. But anyhow, he never did see me. When he did see me, the next thing I knew I was in a Jeep headed over to the main hospital in Bristol. And I spent a week in there. I ended up with the trench-foot ward. They didn't have -- everything was -- in that period of time, the Battle of the Bulge and the trench-foot cases, and they didn't have room. So I went in with a bunch of smelly feet. And it was funny because I had -- when -- before that had happened, I was also moving people on the Tavistock Hospital. We were over there winterizing tents, putting them up and putting framework around, to cover up -- and also stretcher barriers at night. It didn't -- seemed like the damn Red Cross trains would pull in at one o'clock, two o'clock in the morning. And they roused us engineers up to help the medics carry the stretcher cases to the wards. So I had my stay there. And I -- my first sergeant at that point was now Sergeant Litt. He was from Chicago. And he came in at about a day or so, and he said, "You know, we're going to have to leave you behind." And I said, "What do you mean?" He says, "Well, we've got shipping orders to go out." This was January. I said, "Hey, I don't want to miss it." So I got the okay, and I got back one day before we cut. What did -- what did I get? I was assigned baggage detail, which meant I had to load baggage. I had been on my back for a week and here I'm loading bags. Load them on the truck, off-load them onto the train, off-load them off the train onto the trucks, off-load them onto the boat. And we went over on an LCI, and we came in to Le Havre and went up the same river to a staging area. On the trip over, of course I was in the mess hall again. That's when I discovered the Navy lived beautiful. Here was ice cream and steaks. Here I'm passing out 10-in-1 ration food to the troops. So after they got through, I went in and cut myself a nice big steak, had a steak dinner and ice cream again. After we got ashore, back on baggage detail again. And we spent I guess a week, maybe, in January and we motorized up to our new area. We didn't know where we were going. We went up to Belgium in the back side of the Bulge. I say "back side" at that time because they had to start moving away. And the first remembrance of seeing dead Germans and everything, carnage of war, in that same town, St. Vith, was interesting. Because I revisited that town back when I worked in Europe in '68 and I said, "Oh hell, this is the town that didn't have a roof at any place." But we had one can of salmon and one loaf of bread. That was our food for breakfast, lunch, and then we had sea rations when we finally got to -- into Holland. And I traded my -- I had spaghetti. I traded it to a Dutch person for two eggs with my slice of bread. And we then went from there. We motored up the -- what was the Hell's Highway, which the Airborne had called it, when they made the drop. So we followed the road up from Eindhoven, on up to a place up close to Nijmegen, Ireland --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: -- and the Reichswald Forest, ended up in it. On my way up, I had the scare of my life. I looked up and -- I'm sitting in the backseat of the truck and I looked up and here comes an Me-109. I thought, oh, shit. We didn't have any guns on our -- on our -- but luckily there was a Spitfire on his tail. And that Jerry was -- all he was thinking about was getting my fanny back home. So that was a scary moment. Ended up in the Reichswald Forest with a bunch of Canadians and they kidded me. And they said, "You know, we've been shelled out of here three times by the Jerrys for crossing the river." So we were stationed there all the way through until we made the Rhine crossing. And our job then was to widen the roads for the block wave, which are the British trucks, bearing -- bringing up the landing -- assault boats to go across the Rhine River. And we cleared mines and widened the roads, and I can remember that. And then the day of -- stupid things we would do. We would try to set off 500-pound bombs by shooting at them from a safe distance.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What is a safe distance?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Well, looking back at it, I don't know if we were far enough away or not, but at least we did not set anything off. But I did -- we did do one stupid thing. In March, when they made the drop -- Airborne made the drop on a diesel, the drop color, they told us afterwards, was an orange smoke. And here we were playing around with some on this side of the Rhine River, which was orange that day, setting them off just for the hell of it and never realizing we were the same color. This is the story I received, anyway. So we crossed over a good combat engineer outfit -- actually, it was -- they were combat, but they were more construction. They had built a bridge, and we went across on that bridge. And we went down the road and followed it, putting in lampposts -- I shouldn't say lampposts, but putting in trees and painting at the top right -- about a foot wide for the little slits of light you could pick up on the side of the road and so forth. And we had our first casualty. He was a -- he was a fellow we called Frankenstein. He had a face like -- all he was missing was bolts in his head. The guy -- he looked like good old Frankenstein.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And he went up playing around with a Jerry machine gun and put a bullet through his own leg. And I went up there and I heard him -- we heard him yell. Sergeant Clark and I went up. And this stupid character, he didn't even have -- Turney (ph) was his name. He didn't have a -- his first aid kit. So I had -- ripped mine off. We slit his pants, and Clark was bitching like hell. And we closed up -- put a patch on his leg. And it went down there to the calf muscle. And we got him down to the highway and we stopped a British ambulance going back. That was the last we ever saw of this guy. And we continued on into -- into April. I can remember a tanker coming up -- getting in a tanker saying to me, "Hey Yank, your president died yesterday." And that's how I received my president -- didn't -- thought I was in -- we got as far as Bocholt in April, and they -- since I had this drafting experience, the next thing, our outfit was pulled out and we were sent down to Trier to map the region, in the Mosel region, for "Werwolf" activities.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: "Werwolf" activities?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Uh-huh. This was going to be the _____+ that was going to continue the war after it was over. And just recently on TV they had a program on that, which I was part of but didn't know, in the _____ area of -- Hitler's _____ -- I'm trying to -- was where they were most active.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And it continued into July of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. And they -- so I happened to see this on PBS on -- I should say on the History Channel the other day. And boy, it was interesting. Because here I had -- what we did, we worked 16 hours a day, I'm not kidding, with Coleman lanterns. We would send out a Jeep. You had a certain area to patrol. And anyplace we could get a Jeep in, we mapped that as a Jeep path or a truck path.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So if anything came up out of that area, we knew -- would know whether they could get in with Jeeps or trucks or whatever. So we mapped that whole damn area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The only way they could find out if is if they were being shot at or something?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No, no. See, the idea, Werewolf activities would take place in this Mosel area. The infantry had these maps we made, and they knew what the terrain was and everything else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: One of the interesting things in that period of time, after -- right afterwards, we got into a German area after the war and discovered a -- I don't know what you call it -- storage area, which had -- Germans had made a topographical map out of plaster of Paris, squares like this. Everything was true to scale, all the way from the Atlantic Ocean, all the way back. So all these plaques were out -- in this huge room. See, they had a complete thing. And we ended up guarding that down there. So it was interesting in that respect. But it was tiresome. I mean, my eyes would burn. But it was something we had to do. And so we pulled out of there, then. I can remember there was still outfits going up to the front, where we were at, and it was a big highway. There was 240s being pulled by a power pack unit, not a truck. They had their own motorized unit. And finished up doing that. We went over to Ahaus, Germany -- I don't know how I'm doing on that, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're doing --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I haven't heard it click. But anyway, over to Ahaus, Germany and -- I better not go into that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You don't want to go into that?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: No, no. But Ahaus, in that town we ended up all set. We spent a couple of days there. Then we moved up to a place called Ingelheim am Rhein. That's about 20 miles on the Rhine River outside of Mainz. And there we ended -- went into a chemical fact- --Ingelheim Chemical Works. And we -- of course, our -- we ended up bunking in the -- in the office buildings and so forth. They had a German -- the Germans had Russian slave labor working in the camp, and they had con- -- brick buildings for them. And I can remember going into -- seeing that and being told by one Russian -- this was -- we were workers here. And one of the Russians pointed out two of the Germans that had killed American pilots, you know? Ingelheim am Rhein, we had an E-boat on the Rhine River. And one of the things which we -- as we collected mines in that, we used to get a little four-inch dynamite pack. And of course, we would take the boat out, and the Germans were all there with their fishing poles, trying to catch fish. Well, we'd throw a quarter-pound block of TNT, and they'd scoop up the fish and trade it for a bottle of wine or two. I'm not exaggerating. We actually had a chemical bottle. It must have been ten gallons of wine. But we would -- I'd walk down to the Rhine River. That's when the fraternization was "streng verboten." And of course, needless to say, ended up meeting a pal of mine, Ruth Klepal (ph). And MPs would come down along the river and we'd be walking along and they didn't bother us. But in the process down there, in moseying around, I -- they had a cemetery down there, which I found a crew -- a bomber crew had been buried. So when I got back that evening, I told the old man to get a ahold of grave registration, and they went down and they got the bodies. So we did some good in that respect. The other thing I ended up doing is working at the train station. We had set up a water system, which would have a lot of pipes. You'd get troop trains coming through. The guys would get off and get water and canteens and so forth. And of course, all the Germans coming through on their trains would do the same thing too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So instead of staying at -- down at the office in the chemical works, I'd be up sleeping in the train station. And we ended up -- I got back into the cooking a little bit there, and we would take -- we would -- discovered a German who had lived in the United States, New York City, made ice cream. So we would take our big tin cans of orange marmalade, which I detested, into Mainz, and he'd convert it into ice cream for Sunday meals. And it was funny because watching at that period of time, people crossing back over the Rhine River, and when they would come up to cross over to the other side, they had to be DDT'd, spray them all down, lift up your armpits, you know, "Open up your blouse, ma'am," and we powdered them all. And the other thing, I ended up -- we ended up taking care of PWs -- I shouldn't say taking care of PWs. Utilizing them. In Mainz was a German Panzer school during -- in Germany, and it was housing 5,000 DTs. You name it, they had -- we had Russians, we had French, we had Slovaks, we had Polacks, Norweigians, Hollanders, French. And that was interesting because there, the sewer works had been destroyed. And I -- one of the things I really -- I got -- I can remember the first words of French I started learning was, for me, "les robinets," turn off the faucets, because of the water.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But they went to -- the French didn't seem to have any partiality to using the slit trenches or the latrines. And by Christ, they actually defecated right in the rooms up there, set a room aside. That was messy. But -- so we went -- they -- prisoner of war camp was over at Heidesheim, and it was on the side of a hill. And we probably had 80,000. And the weather was miserable and these guys had nothing. So we went -- we tried to get the -- we went in there and we got the able-bodied Germans to -- in the truck, and we'd take them into the barracks in Mainz and have them work build -- rebuilding the sewer system. Well, one of the problems was, we had a few thousand Italians. They'd get up on the barracks, three-story barracks, and throw stones down at the Germans. Of course I was down there too. So we got to the point where we would fire a couple of rounds over their heads. But I can remember, you know, here we were driving with these Germans in the truck. I'm in the tailgate and my buddy is on the other side, and we had maybe 30 German PWs. And the civilians would toss out the German black loaf of -- German black bread. You're doing 30 miles an hour. And a loaf of black bread coming, weighing a pound, was a missile. END OF CD ONE; BEGIN CD TWO

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And this is where the -- another one of the problems I got with my platoon sergeant from Detroit; name was Sergeant Schwab. And we were sitting at the lunch hour break, and people were coming up to the fence and they were trying to put food to the soldiers because they were starving, really. And there was an article later on I read about mistreatment of Eisenhower; he was so anti-German. Some of the people that we released to work, the British said they weren't capable of working. And we had -- they were maltreated and so forth. That was another part hidden in the archives of history. But anyhow, I can remember sitting there, and the people were bringing up cherries, canned cherries. They were trying to pass through knives and forks. And I would say, "Messers und Gabel verboten." "Geben den Löffel," the spoon. And they could eat and set it all up. But this Sergeant Schwab, he was an SOB and he was anti -- I said, "Now wait a minute. We're eating." Let -- if the people want to give them food, as long as it's, you know, not going to hurt us, let them -- let them have something. Because I knew it -- we knew -- I knew full well they weren't getting -- they were suffering on that hillside in Hildesheim. But anyway, it ended up that we had to drop the Germans because of the recon. So we went in and we said, "A pack of cigarettes if you work here." He wouldn't work for that. They were just going to eat and they'd be comfortable. So we ended up forcing them to come out and work.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Italians?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. We were forcing them to come out. So they'd be, "I'm drunk, I'm sick, malad." So then we brought the medic in, medical officer in, and we actually -- I mean, you had an interesting period of seeing how people were -- and by far, the cleanliest people by far in Europe was the Dutch, the Hollander. They'd -- there'd be one body there and they'd be washing the street down -- the sidewalk down. And that was another interesting thing, which going up to the front, outside of Maastricht, there was a side of a house painted, "Good luck, Yanks." And then when we came back after there, later, "Thank you" on the other side of the house coming back. So I'm jumping around a little bit there. But it was interesting. I really had an admiration for the Dutch people. And as I say, we went from there. The area east of the -- west of the Rhine was being turned over to the French. So we ended up going out of there up to a place called Metzingen up in Northeast Germany. This was a hospital town for German soldiers. Boy, were we hated. Because you had every -- everything happen; plates in the heads and arms missing, limbs -- well, limbs missing, you know. Horrendous. So that was a town that was -- but I did learn to drink "kartoffel" beer, which is potato beer. It's sweet. But after two glasses, even being cold, that was enough. So that was starting into July. August, we motored down. We got transferred. And the 288th, we went south, down to Patton's Third Army. I got sick and spent a couple of days at Stuttgart Hospital. And we finally ended up in Ingolstadt, in Bavaria. And at that point, our outfit got broken up. I only had 52 points, so I wasn't going home. And I got transferred, I think, over -- I'm not certain what the outfit was. I think it was 140th Combat Engineers, something like that. And then we finally started on convoy to the ports. And the war ended when I was in Kaiserslautern, Germany, in the French area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you potentially headed for the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh, yes. That's where I was headed for.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, that's -- I got transferred into 140th Combat Engineers, and we were heading for the Pacific and the war ended. So we ended up in Camp Washington for a few weeks. And it was interesting, because there I got on water detail again, which was going around putting chlorine in the various bags for the pumping system in that camp. Then I got a couple of passes into Paris for a couple of days and then came back and the outfit moved up to Le Havre, France, Camp Twenty Grand. What was I doing there? We were making provisions for guys coming back to ship out to go back to the States, then, at that point, because they were unloading Europe with soldiers. I ended up with a detail of -- I mean, to maintain flow of sand, gravel, for mixture for -- because we put down concrete patch for the squad tents. And after a while there, next thing we know, we got transferred again, up to a place called Vilvoorde, Belgium, which is outside of Brussels, oh, about ten miles, I would say. And it was on a -- it was used for the 9th Combat -- 9th Air Force used that field. And went in there. I'm trying to remember what the heck I did in Vilvoorde right now. Like I said, I ended up back working in the mess hall, and we had German help all the way through. I had a sergeant, myself, and a Mexican kid from New Mexico. He was, I would say, old Army, only because he had gone in before the war. But he'd been broken a few times and -- but he and I didn't get along worth a damn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And anyway, they finally said, "Well, you're going to be a T5," a corporal cook, and the other guy was likewise. So we were even up as far as rank went. Then when the first sergeant -- when the mess sergeant got transferred back to the States, I ended up having it. I can remember doing a Christmas meal in Belgium and a Christmas meal I had done in England, so -- and it worked out. The PWs I had were real good. One fellow was a braumeister, and he was the oldest guy. Boy, why can't I remember his name. And he told me he was a "braumeister"; a brewmaster, in other words. And I had another guy, a real intelligent fellow and he was from Eastern Germany. And I got along real well him. "____________?" "Yeah." And that's another thing too. When we were closing up, we were taking stuff and putting it on the trains and shipping it to -- and the Russians were taking it to Russia. We were stripping Germany of their goods at one point. And I can remember the girls that were picking through the stuff would look up at this one -- our corporal at that time was a Jewish fellow. And I could hear them saying "Juden." And then she'd look at -- they looked at my name: "Deutsch-Namen, ja?" "Deutsch." But -- so anyhow, I spent Christmas as a cook there and we got -- trying to think. January, we got sent back. We got holed up there in Operation Vilvoorde. And by the way, Vilvoorde then became Caterpillar's warehouse area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Service center. I ended up over in Belgium later, in '68, and here I'm in Vilvoorde. Gee, how things go around and come around. But anyhow, we shipped up to a place called Tongres. Well, having been -- everything went up there. I mean, all our goods were unloaded up there, brought a three-quarter-ton truck back. And the -- our -- my captain said to me, he says, "You're familiar with what's in -- cooking equipment." He said, "How about staying on?" So I stayed on with all my stuff up there. I only had the clothes on my back. And so I ended up getting clothes out of -- being recycled. And I spent two extra weeks and New Year's in Brussels, Belgium. Christmas, I was broke. I had enough for two beers. But came New Year's, I was loaded. And I had two bottles of scotch, which was the last time I ever drank scotch. And everybody who saw me that day down at the beer -- at the variety cafe couldn't believe I got back the next day. But I -- boy, I was bombed. And I was off, at least, New Year's Day. But I stayed on, and then we finally got back up. My footlocker had been broken into. I had a plywood footlocker with a lock on it. But the -- we were a bunch of winos at that point, Calvados victims.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And they had no voice at all. They were hoarse from drinking in Calvados. And they would swipe everything in order to trade it in Tongres for the Calvados. So I had lost my pistol. That was another story I should have told you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's okay out of sequence.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, okay. But it was interesting. It was the first time in Germany, when we crossed over. And I -- me and my two buddies, we were -- Swanstrom again; I can't remember the other fellow -- walking through this town. I think it was Kirschberg or something like that. And that's the first time I saw my first two dead Jerrys already being wheeled out. And walking through, this young lady came out and called me over. I don't speak German. But I go into the house. I slung my rifle down into -- noncombative, walked in, and they had a coal lamp inside and that whole family is sitting on the couch. And she walks over and comes back, and she's got a pistol. Her "bruder." She said "Mein bruders." And so she gave it to me because they were supposed to surrender the weapons. So she gave me a Browning .765. I came out of there and I say, "I've got a -- I've got one of my first weapons." And the -- I said -- you know, normally I was scared shitless. But that got stolen. It was in my footlocker. They broke in, these guys. So when I got back, my German blanket, my German raincoat -- and the German raincoat came down to here so water didn't get into your boots. It was on your feet. They swiped that, and I was pretty much clothed without clothes to speak of in that. But anyhow, we'd spent the time. I got myself transferred to detach service. In other words, instead of being in the mainland, I got sent up to Roermond, Holland and -- pulling the gas pipes out of Germany and load them up on the truck and then take them back to the harbor, into Antwerp. In the process, I met a very nice Dutch girl. And I think the story -- if I have to say anything, it was probably my real first love. And God, I didn't know her too long, but we corresponded, dated in that period of time. And I can remember the -- I got -- I got -- my orders got cut, shipped back to the States. I didn't want to go and leave her, but my -- at that time, my father had cancer and he was unemployed; the company had fired him. So it was imperative that I not -- so I shipped out of -- out of Belgium, out of Antwerp in February, and arrived back in the States in -- I don't know, maybe the 3rd or so. I don't know. Went down to Camp Kilmer -- let's see. Vilvoorde and Tongres, Holland in March. I come back to the States, yeah. At least I have that all marked down. And of course, the time we off-loaded, there was no ceremony in New York at that time. You know, here it is March. The war has been -- we came back on a ship called the USS Uster -- I'm saying Uster because we had a Scandinavian Captain. ________+. And we shipped out on the tail end of a gale blowing through and everybody was seasick. And I didn't catch a detail. But I went down below deck to see -- to the mess hall. And I said, "Hey, got any apples?" And I went up, and the guy looked up at me and he says -- all these guys puking all over because the -- because the ship is rolling like hell. "And you want apples so you don't get seasick?" And I'm up on the bow, wind blowing in my face. And at that time too, in the last part of Belgium, I picked up scabies. I don't know if you're familiar with that. Like bedbugs, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Another term for them, maybe. But anyhow, I had the lotion. So when we shipped out, I had this lotion I put on daily. Got back to the States, _____+. Got into Camp Kilmer, a German PW is serving us steaks. Of course, the only thing wrong with those steaks, getting back, the steaks were all cold. We arrived at 9:30 at night. But we stayed there a couple of days and then they shipped me over to Camp Atterbury, Indiana, and I went through the debriefing process and so forth. I came back with a duffle bag. I bet it wasn't a quarter full. I didn't have any clothes or anything because I lost everything because of the -- being rifled up in Belgium. I get all the way through, and my discharge says one thing and at the end of day -- interesting looking at that. It says March 11th. And I say, "I didn't get out of Atterbury until March 15th." Well, there was a story to it. When I got through, the medical officer saw the little marks on my wrist. "Oh, you can't leave. You've got to go back for medical treatment." I said, "I've been on medical treatment all the way back on this ship. I says, "I've been doing these. I don't have it." Well, so it says here the 11th of March being discharged. Well, 13th was the real date. And got out of there, and they assigned me -- I was stupid enough to sign up for the Reserves for three years. Thank God nothing happened. And three days later I met my wife-to-be on March 16th. That was my military. It got me that far. And of course 1949 came. I was out of the Reserves. Korean War broke out. Thank God I was out of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But that was my military. So I had come back to try to get on the GI bill for flying and I got turned down because they said I couldn't use it. I was back with Towmotor working again. So finished up my career life with Towmotor. Caterpillar bought us in '65. And '68, took a trip to -- went back to Belgium working for Caterpillar, and we set up a lift-truck operation in Gosselies, Belgium. And I lived in Waterloo. So I had experience going back and retracing the steps where I had been in the Reichswald Forest. And the Ger -- the British had taken all their bodies and -- that were killed, and buried them and had a big cemetery up there. And one of the things I did do, my cousin was in the Battle of the Bulge. And he got killed in the -- December 22nd. My aunt and uncle -- my aunt and uncle and his wife had asked me if I could get up to Henri-Chapelle Cemetery and really see if it was Russell there. Of course, I did. I made a trip back in August of '45, had three days and went up there, saw the cross. The -- there was dog tags on the back of it. And we had 17,000 Jerrys on one side of the hedgerow and something like 12,000 Americans on the other side. And they were exhuming graves up there at that time. And boy, the smell of death was still in the air. And it ended up that I verified Russell. So since then, I've been back to Henri-Chapelle graves monument. People make these huge cemetery complexes, very beautiful memorial type of things. And so I saw his last resting place in there. And -- but being over there afterwards, '68 through '71, I visited Margraten. One of the things, Henri-Chapelle Cemetery took all the battle -- everybody, up until December 31st, was buried in Belgium. But all soldiers after that were buried in Margraten, Holland, outside of Maastricht. So I've traveled to about five or six of the various cemeteries, all beautiful places. I've been, you know, to Normandy and then Luxembourg, where Patton was buried and Margraten, Henri-Chappelle. So -- even saw some of the old lowlands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I bet.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm curious. You mentioned getting a lot of those letters from your girlfriend. What happened to her?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: In -- where?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The girlfriend you were getting -- you said a girlfriend in the States was writing to you when you were --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- overseas?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. The whole thing, though, when I came home that weekend -- and some weekends we never got together. And that's what left me available on the 16th of the month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were available?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Well, yeah. My brother got this phone call from -- his wife was a nurse. She graduated from Humred Hospital. And she was in the nurses training program, part of the government training program. So when they passed the state boards, it was customary to go down and rent a room in Hotel Hollenden and celebrate. Well, my brother knew Frannie well, who was one of the other nurses, and she called my brother up and said they were down in the Hotel Hollenden and so forth. And I was home, and my brother said, "Why don't you go with me? Dad will give you the car." So that's how I ended up --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's how you ended up.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: There's -- that's the Dutch girl.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ah. So you'd -- the Dutch girl, you didn't consider bringing her over as a --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: We -- oh, yes. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think about that?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. If I can find the right one. But I don't know if I can find it. I don't know -- "Do you remember my aunt's" -- this is the Dutch gal I was very serious with, and this is all the -- this church from our village. Here is aunt's farm, where Allied airmen were hidden --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: -- and brought back into the underground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So -- and various things here. I got pictures of -- from the Germans they left behind. And so this is a view from the village, _____. You came through it when you came by -- from -- to Roermond. So anyhow, this is the church and so forth. "Do you remember my aunt's house and so forth and so on? I am sure you'll remember this bridge. Don't you?" Because I must have crossed over it and -- to visit with her. And that was my picture taken in conjunction with this other one, as you can see. But, oh, God. It -- I think that's the first time that I can say I was really involved and -- but she -- we corresponded. And she was wiser than I. She spoke five languages. She was a lieutenant in the Dutch Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Indonese, French, German, English. And, oh, as I say, much time as I could spend with her, I did. And it -- when something -- but she said, "It's not going to work out." And at the -- of course, the time really elapsed from the time I saw her, leaving Belgium, leaving her in February and shipping back. We corresponded, and she said -- she even said if I could have stayed there, she -- her dad would have got me a job in the railroad. But it was -- she had realized after a few months that this was not going, of course. And in the interim I had met the wife-to-be. And -- but I actually visited her since. I saw her in 1969, and she was married -- of all things, she married a German.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And she had a son and daughter. And I lost -- needless to say, I've lost track of her.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Well, I have since that time. I sent -- I gave her my business card and I said, "If you ever want to correspond with me, send it through Caterpillar here and they'll forward it to me in the States." And that was back in, as I say, '69. So I'm still sort of curious. I'd like to return. I've got a beautiful -- another beautiful picture of her, which is in my souvenirs downstairs, in a sterling silver frame. I'd like to return it to her daughter or son. But I don't have a real good working address for her. That's the only thing. But that was -- that was -- this was the place where they had the -- I don't know if I can -- hosting -- the Rhine Holstein area. This is the castle, Rhine Holstein. This is where I had all these topographical plaster of Paris area. This is us guys going through some of the stuff in Germany, the first place. And it's ironic. You can see we went through -- and the Jerrys had sort of dumped everything in the process. And I got -- all I got -- I took a few applets off of a beautiful German officer's uniform. But I got little coins and -- from -- in -- lying in there. I also got some beautiful Dutch coins, which are pure silver, like our old money used to be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So anyhow, that's where this happened. I've re -- went back to try to find -- I went back there and tried to find Heinz _____. And I got down to the town in Germany where -- which I had his address, and I don't have it. Oh, it's in the other book. And went to the police station and I told them I was looking for this fellow. And every -- in Europe, the police station is the source and -- or the church, for information. And when I -- I can remember speaking with this fellow. I said he was a brewmaster. He says, "Anyone who works in a brewery is a brewmaster." Well, when they pulled a card on him, it said -- he said, "Well, he was a brewmaster, but he's tot." He's dead. So he gave me the address of his wife. And by God, I went over in '68 and saw his family and told him who I was. And they accepted me. Because one of the things, at Christmas in Belgium with these guys, I went out and got three bottles of red wine for the three of us. Now, Heinz was the bossman. The other fellow was from east Russia, and myself. And I went out and got ten gallons of two -- ten gallons of beer for the rest of the guys for the Christmas Eve celebration. So I was really remembered by the family that this is the American. But as I say, it was rather disappointing. Then I went back and looked up this gal in Ingelheim. And that was another disappointment. I mean, when I went into the town, I said -- with my -- with my limited German I had picked up, I said -- what did I say in German? "I'm looking for the Klepal (ph) family." And the person says -- pointed in there, and you went in through an arched wall. And a house was in the back and a house was in the front. Well, this gal went running in and got ahold of Ruth saying, "There's an American, an American here, an America looking for you." Well, Ruth comes rushing down the stairs, and I was astounded because -- Ruth was a tall girl, blonde hair, oh, about 140, -50 pounds when I knew her. And she weighed 200 pounds, wore -- had a T-shirt, holes in it. She was worse off than when I knew her after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: It was a disappointment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And my family was sitting in the car outside and the kids said, "Oh, Dad is looking up one of his old -- one of his old girls." But no, that was the thing. So I -- I've seen Ruth, I've seen Gerta, the two that really had meaning in my life. And I still have a deep feeling for this Gerta.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I don't know. I've been married over 57 years, but now I'm a full-time caregiver.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So... I think she's finally gone down again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah. So anyhow --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did a good job of covering it.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, and probably missed quite a bit too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories that come to mind when you were thinking about this?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Vivid memories? No, not really. I can remember trying to blow up a German house with all the munitions that were in it by pulling a -- put a string in a German potato masher, and the string broke and I laid down. In the end, I was going to get down just to see where it was. So that place was booby-trapped, as far as I was concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was just left like that?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, it was left like that. No, it was surprising. Because getting the chance to go back in '68 working for Caterpillar and able to travel -- and it was funny. The bridge -- I crossed over the Rhine River. One of the -- one of the trips -- one of the kids -- we were in Germany, and there was gliders coming in and making landings. And I walked over, and it was right outside of _____. I said to the people, I says -- they were asking about the wooden bridge. Because we came across this beautiful concrete bridge. And he says, oh, yeah, that was built two years in _____. And he said the _____ bridge, brücke, had lasted until 1966 --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: -- which was put up in '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And they had used it until they put this bridge. So that was interesting, because that was a hell of a high bridge going over the Rhine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And it was a good, good construction outfit that put it up and it stood all those years. And that was a memorable type of thing. Plus, you know, you've gone back and you looked up places you'd been. And like I said, the Reichswald Forest, to discover the British Canadians being buried there. And I was asked by my aunt, my -- by Russ's wife, "If you had been killed, would you want your body brought back or left there?" And I -- my feeling was, if I had been killed over there, I'd want to be buried there. And so his body was left behind. And a lot of people brought them back. But I can remember what I had seen in August, buried in December, and August eight months later, that was a heck of a lot you were bringing back. It's like these Vietnam -- you're in a casket. Hell, you're -- what, for five, six grand? It doesn't make sense.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But anyhow, I saw -- I talked to an Amish fellow, talked to the guy. And that was another thing. His sergeant wrote and said he was machine-gunned, killed by machine gun fire. And the other aspect was, his outfit was still in Danzig, in Belgium, when Belgium was owned. They were in the upper -- northern part. And when they got back -- got in there, I went down and looked at the grave registration house and they had to report to them that said shellfire, cannon got them, shrapnel. And they listed what positions he had. Because his wedding band was taken and that was never returned. So we -- that was confiscated, if you can use that term, liberated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But I made it, so I found out actually how he was killed and -- where -- but no, you look back on all these things and all you can say is we spent a hell of a lot of money on graves.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And people don't realize -- and when you -- when you're in wartime, you're put in a sleeping bag, which is cotton, and you're put into the ground. And if you're -- it doesn't take long for the ground to dissolve. And I can remember -- being in there, watch a guy pull out. "Yeah, we have three hands in this grave," he says. "We're trying to figure out which two go together," you know?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And it's just like JELL-O. I don't know if I explained. You take JELL-O and you put your spoon into it, and it sort of peels apart. The flesh is black, and it peels -- it pulls off from the bone, just like it was JELL-O. But I don't know. I lucked out. I was in the worst outfit you could ever be in, and it's surprising. Were we in luck with Montgomery's Army, Ninth Army up there, 1st -- 21st Group, and we got a detail of maintaining bridges, widening the roads, and clearing a few mines? We could have been up -- even up front putting those bridges across, and here we got that duty. It was the luckiest part of the war for me, as far as I'm concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And, you know, how many -- I go through here now. I can -- Captain Herkenrath (ph) was my captain. And I can remember him moaning in Ingelheim about going home. He was a lawyer, by the way, from Milwaukee. And he was moaning about it when we're on ranks out there for retreat, and I could hear him. And, of course an officer had to be served after the war. They had -- you had -- _____. They were out of canteens, but the officers -- so -- I got that -- sort of that duty for that -- maintaining that. But he was bitching about going home. Of course, we were all sitting in the ranks bitching too, listening to him. But Lieutenant Stuck was a hell of a good guy, and Captain Herkenrath (ph) was an okay officer, I guess. I've got pictures, and I can't -- I don't remember their names. It's ironic that certain people stood out. And Butler was the other first sergeant we had in this 280 Comp. His -- Germans took pictures of their girlfriends and so forth. And the first time we liberated -- or it wasn't liberal. The first time I was in going through the stuff, I got some of his stuff. Not much. But it was the type of thing -- they're human. And -- well, here was the -- here was the officer's group. But -- I've got a picture of the _____ you seen here. And the only guy -- I recognize Reese. And he was a -- he had gone in the Service in '37, so he was over in Hawaii and came back to the States before Pearl Harbor. And he was -- and some of the names I remember and -- mess sergeant, when -- Higginbotham. I went out and visited him in '47, on our second honeymoon. And he died a year later, cancer. Buck Sergeant Vectiem (ph), he was -- Michigan, and he's dead. He died real quick, right after the war. And, you know, Schwab, Norm Swanstrom. Pop Chambers. The only reason I remember Pop Chambers, he was 50 years of age and he was in our outfit. What the hell is a 50-year-old man -- except he had eight kids. He had -- was making more money being in the Service. But they discharged him finally. He was in Kentucky, and he didn't have any education and he worked in the mess hall. They had a picture of him but -- on camp outfit. But it was strange. Oh, that's the other thing I started figuring. Why did I have two serial numbers?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did you have two serials?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Uh-huh. That was one of the things which really bugged me and bugged me and bugged me. Because if you look at -- my first serial number I was given was 3556190. Now, as of September, I still had it. Now, if you flip over one page over and it's still there, and that was still there on September 19th, and it was still there in the two letters from Doris on the 19th, still October, October. And October 18th, 35048294. You subtract from 356190 [sic], you'll find that it's 487,000 numbers different. You know, I often wondered why I was the youngest guy in my area going into the Service. Because I had -- I was the youngest -- the older guys, by a year or two, came in months -- a couple, three to four months after me. And you cannot get from the government who that -- that number. I think somehow the draft board got me early, before the other guys. I had a Slovenian draft board, I have a feeling, because the other names were either Slovenian, Samole, Dow English, Scotch English. But I was 400,000 difference. And why did they change in October before I -- going overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Jeez.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Now, that bugs the living devil out of me. I have tried to figure that out. I've wrote and asked for information on it. And they said, "All we could tell you, that number was assigned in December of '42." But to who? So that was one of the -- I even went down to the archives in St. Louis, but they wouldn't give you -- they wouldn't give you the information.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They wouldn't?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: I would have loved to -- see, that's the Fifth Army command in Ohio. And what else? But -- and then Fort Harrison, Columbus was the headquarters for the Fifth -- Fifth thing. And I thought, jeez, I'd like to find out -- I could ask the guy when he went in Service then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Who got my old number.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I haven't been able to get that. And of course, a lot of the records have been destroyed in the fires too that they had. But I finally sent in for my ribbons, et cetera, and found out I got an Army of Occupation of Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I never knew I -- I knew what was in -- you know, gosh, I didn't get out of there until September or August, and so that was actually Army of Occupation at that point. But -- so I got a set of medals, you know, and ribbons, and that. And surprisingly enough, I got -- the second set came about four months later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Good old -- good old Americans. We know not what we doeth. But it was surprising. I -- as I say, I had -- I went south, never went north with the military, and then -- overseas. But it's surprising. One of my buddies I was raised with, I saw he -- he had a reunion. I called Norm up. We were -- we lived on the same street, four years of age, went to high school together, graduated high school. And he went -- he was in combat engineers. He said, "Oh, I was on the Commodore ship." And I says, "You were shipped." And I said, "You went in to Swansea, Wales." He got a pass into -- into New York City. That was the interesting part. He got a pass. And another one of my classmates from Clermont High School, '41, went with them. Anyway, I found out when talking with Norm. And ironically, where I worked with Towmotor Lift Trucks, he worked for Baker Raulang Lift Trucks. But his outfit got marched all the way up to the front, and they were up in the front lines and he ended up inside of Germany quite a bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Whereas I -- there again, I pulled back to do mapmaking and -- for the "Werwolf" activities. But he said he -- he got into the Hummel factory. He said, "I got a few souvenirs out of Hummel." Hummel made tanks.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Soldiers. You know, the dolls, but they also made military stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize that.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Yeah, back in the war for the Germans. So he got some souvenirs. And I haven't met up with him in -- now, here's a fellow I -- right here. I talked to him. He and I were best of buddies. He was a little bit younger than I, about a year. And I said, "Jim, get in the Air Corps." And he and I ended up in University of Tennessee for about three weeks together. He was straight Air Corps; as you can see, captain. Now, he -- where he got killed, on a mission out of Wright Patterson Field, he was flying a 29 with a hook on the belly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: A hook on the belly was the old Crucible days. And the planes -- the Crucibles carried their own planes on a hook.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: He got cut in half by a Ranger flying a P47 with a hook on it. He flew right through the 29. PA4 Thunderbird fighter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So Jim went down in -- off of Long Island. But as I say, he was my best buddy. So anyhow, yep, I -- at least I got -- if I had gotten my wings, I know full -- I would have been in for 20 years or better. But to be turned down by the government for trying to get my commercial stuff, I had enough hour -- enough time in. And the guy living on the street from me was an instructor and he said, "Hey, you know, I can guarantee you I'll get you a commercial pilot's license." And the government said I couldn't use it because I was back in drafting and they turned me down and I've never got a damn thing from the government. No GI Bill; I didn't use it. I tried to get GI loans; they were not available. So I don't feel the USA -- I owe them any more than I've given them. And my -- like the other part, my son, he went into the -- enlisted in the Vietnam period with his buddy. And I said, okay, that's three generations of Sweigerts. I think that's enough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So Tom, that is, I don't know more I can say to you. But I did find one thing downstairs. I found my shipping orders.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, you did?

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh, yeah. These guys were all privates unless otherwise mentioned, it says. Archives. 63rd Headquarters, University of Tennessee, Knoxville. Unless otherwise so ordered, these are all privates. Sweigert, Ernest C., 35 -- now, why -- there it is. There it is. That's before October. There it is there. I knew damn well that I had that early.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I saw I was either still using 3 -- that was in September. We were still using it, but yet I -- here I was in the University of Tennessee under the -- I knew full well -- I remember I got that new number in Keesler Field, I'm positive. I stood in the ranks and the guy called out "Sweigert" and I answered 6190. "Not you." And I was the last guy standing in the -- in the field, and he says, "What in the hell is your name?" I said, "Sweigert." I says, "6190." He says, "No" and he quartered to me right there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And that's when I got my new number, in Keesler Field, when I went into the Air Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There you go.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: So why?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is --

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: Oh, by the way, too, if you came on the ground forces, you were -- you were called aviation student, not aviation cadet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: And I think that was one way they kept track of me -- kept track of the guys in rank and so forth. This is the fellow that got washed out right here. You notice the garb we were wearing, winter flying equipment. And so this is when -- we were up there in February, March. Water froze in the taps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ah, jeez.

sp.speaker: Ernest C. Sweigert
sp.p: But this is Chuck Schroeder. And where in the hell is Atkinson? Murphy was his name, JJ Murphy and I, Decatur, Alabama, March '44. And here's Atkinson right here from Hawaii. And man, could he fly. So these two guys made it. I didn't. I got cut, and he got cut way back, as I say. Ah, innocence of youth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.
